Thanks again for taking the time today — great discussion. Quick recap from our discovery focused on performance and autoscaling requirements so we have alignment before Ben and I propose a pilot. If I missed anything, flag it and we’ll update.

High-level asks you shared:
- Interactive customer-facing chat: target P95 latency ~150ms for short prompts (<=200 tokens).
- Sustained throughput: 200-300 concurrent users during peak; typical peak duration ~15-30 minutes.
- Streaming required: partial response streaming for first tokens within 100-200ms.
- Burst capacity: ability to handle 2-3x baseline for 10-20 minute bursts.
- Maximum acceptable queueing: 30s for requests in extreme bursts (prefer <15s).
- Warm pool preference: keep a small warm pool for critical endpoints to avoid cold-starts; scale-up time target <= 90s.

Follow-ups from our side:
1) We’ll validate scale-up behavior with a dedicated pilot (warm pools + autoscale) and share a test plan.
2) Dev will outline pre-warm sizing, expected cold start characteristics, and queueing backpressure semantics.
3) Commercial: Ben will propose pilot pricing + measurement windows and success criteria.

Attachments: SLO_requirements.xlsx (draft SLO table), AMPLIFY-scale-diagram.png (high-level architecture).

Next steps / proposed dates:
- Technical pilot kickoff: week of Feb 22 (pilot runs 2 weeks)
- Joint scale test: within 1 week of kickoff
- Review pilot metrics and decide on Dedicated pool commit: 2/22 + 2 weeks run

Marissa — thanks for the clear notes. Couple quick clarifications from our side: 

- P95: 150ms for short prompts sounds right as the goal, but we can tolerate up to 250ms during bursts for non-critical flows. Critical flows (authenticating trader alerts) must stay below 200ms P95.
- Concurrency: expect 200-300 concurrent active sessions for customers; internal batch jobs could add another ~50 requests per second but are lower priority.
- Streaming: yes — streaming is required; clients will render partial tokens as they arrive, so first-byte latency is important.
- Bursts: 2-3x baseline is a good target; most bursts come from market-open windows (10-15 minutes).
- Queueing: prefer graceful degradation (queue + informative retry headers) over immediate failures. Queue window 30s max is acceptable.

Also: what does Redwood consider a "warm" worker? Is that a fully loaded model instance with KV cache primed or something lighter? That distinction matters for our sizing.

We’re generally ok with the Feb 22 kickoff; Ben, can you confirm pilot commercial terms?

—Ruth

Subject: Re: Performance SLOs & Autoscaling — technical details on warm pools & scaling

Hi Ruth — quick technical reply to the "warm" question and how we typically run pilots. Happy to dive deeper in a tech call (I can join).

What we mean by warm:
- Warm instance = model worker with weights loaded, kernels initialized, KV cache unpopulated (cold for prompt-specific context).
- Warm+prefill = we can pre-warm with common prefixes for your top flows so KV cache has some hot entries (useful if prompts are highly repetitive).

Scale-up behavior (summary):
- Scale-up time to a warm worker (capacity increase by adding warm instance): ~20-45s depending on instance type and region.
- Cold-start to first-token for new instance (load + init): ~60-120s; we avoid user-facing cold-starts by maintaining a configurable warm pool.
- Autoscaling policy options: instance-based (add X workers), queue-based (spin up when queue length > threshold), or predictive (pre-warm based on schedule/traffic forecasts).
- Queueing/backpressure: requests are queued with exponential backoff headers; we surface X-Queue-Position and X-Estimated-Wait headers. We recommend soft limits (drop low-priority/background requests first) if queue > configured maximum.

Pilot test plan (high level):
1) Baseline run (no warm pool) - measure cold-start behavior for typical prompt sizes.
2) Warm-pool run - size warm pool for target concurrency and measure P95/P99 and first-byte times.
3) Burst test - replay synthetic burst traffic (2-3x baseline) and measure scale-up time, queue length, and token throughput.

I attached the recent internal scale test results we ran (scale-test-results.csv) and a simple sizing calc in SLO_requirements.xlsx. For your first pass I'd size a warm pool of 30 workers for the 200-300 concurrent sessions target; we can adjust after the baseline run.

Let me know if you want me to run an annotated test with your infra team on Feb 24 (we'll need a short network-fingerprint test first).
